#### The payment pipeline — stack and heap at every step

**What is being answered.** Why the dedup shuffle does not save this pipeline — as a crash that is traced through the one line that matters.

`crash(pipe)` is the step to read twice: it returns `Pipeline(pipe.offset, [])`. The **offset survives** because it was committed; the **seen-set does not** because it was in memory. So the replay re-reads record 4 *and* the shuffle thinks it is new.

Everything then rests on `charge`'s early return, which reads `proc.chargedKeys` — the only state that lived outside the crashed process. With it: 6. Without it: 12.

The animation steps through the code, holding each line long enough to read the STACK (call frames and their locals) and the HEAP (allocated arrays and objects) as they are AT THAT MOMENT. Expand any step to study it on its own.

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-system-memory/ch05-system-memory.svg" alt="The payment pipeline — stack and heap at every step, 4 steps showing stack and heap" width="980">

<details>
<summary><b>Step 1 of 4</b> — pass 1 — the dedup set admits it, and the charge lands</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-system-memory/frames/step-01.svg" alt="Step 1: pass 1 — the dedup set admits it, and the charge lands" width="980">

`pipe.seen` is empty, so the record is admitted, and the key is built from `e.id` — `"order-4"`, derived from the data. `totalCharged` goes 0 → 6. Everything about this pass is correct, which is the point: the problem is entirely in what happens next.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 2 of 4</b> — the crash takes the seen-set and leaves the offset</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-system-memory/frames/step-02.svg" alt="Step 2: the crash takes the seen-set and leaves the offset" width="980">

`seen` becomes `[]` while `offset` stays 4. That asymmetry is the whole scenario: the offset was durable and the dedup set was in memory, so the replay will re-read record 4 AND the shuffle will think it is new. The dedup guard is gone exactly when it is needed.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 3 of 4</b> — pass 2 — dedup lets it through, and the KEY stops it</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-system-memory/frames/step-03.svg" alt="Step 3: pass 2 — dedup lets it through, and the KEY stops it" width="980">

`contains(pipe.seen, 4)` is false — the set was cleared — so `sinkWrite` calls `charge` again. The processor's `chargedKeys` still holds "order-4", so it returns early and `totalCharged` stays 6. The guarantee came from the one piece of state outside the pipeline.

</details>
<details>
<summary><b>Step 4 of 4</b> — and without the key the same run charges 12</summary>

<img src="../diagrams/anim/ch05-system-memory/frames/step-04.svg" alt="Step 4: and without the key the same run charges 12" width="980">

`doubled` = 6 — a full second charge. Read the two heap rows: identical pipelines, identical crash, and the only difference is whether the processor remembered the key across it. That is why the key is the mechanism and the dedup shuffle is an optimisation.

</details>
